raw_comment:
1. From 1980 to 2013, the average temperature during summer has risen rapidly. In addition, hot days and extremely hot days account for more than half of the whole data. In fact, the brutal heat continued day after day last year. According to my junior high school Japanese teacher, temperatures over 30 degrees were extremely rare when he was a child. 
2. I wonder why the average temperature during summer rose rapidly. I think the various developments around the world worsened global warming.  I also wonder why the data showed a wider range of temperature differences for about 30 years. 
3. If the average temperature in summer continues to rise, many people will get heat stroke. Especially, there are many elderly people in Akita, where I live, so the preventive measures should be necessary. 
4. Catchy Headline : Protect Ourselves From Extreme Heat!

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

In fact, the brutal heat continued day after day last year. According to my junior high school Japanese teacher, temperatures over 30 degrees were extremely rare when he was a child. 
2. I wonder why the average temperature during summer rose rapidly. I think the various developments around the world worsened global warming.  I also wonder why the data showed a wider range of temperature differences for about 30 years. 
3. If the average temperature in summer continues to rise, many people will get heat stroke. Especially, there are many elderly people in Akita, where I live, so the preventive measures should be necessary. 
4. Catchy Headline : Protect Ourselves From Extreme Heat!

- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

|---|---|---|

| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
I notice that the heat temperature has risen significantly. The frequency of extremely hot summers as gone from barely any to making up a significant portion of the total years sampled. The summers are also more varied. In the 1951-1980 graph, the summers are very concentrated at one peak, but that peak turns into more of a hill with how spread the temperatures are. It also appears that the entire first standard deviation or so from the mean fits into the hot section of the graph, instead of being centered over the normal. I do wonder how many degrees of temperature away from normal is considered extreme. Is it +- 5°c? +- 1°c? The graph calling it "Extremely hot" or "Extremely cold" could be mostly sensationalism. But I agree that the temps have been getting hotter. Each summer seems hotter than the last, even throughout just the past 10 years.

"Turning Up The Heat: How our summers have intensified in 72 years"

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
	In the first graph , from 1951-1980, I noticed that the normal, cold, and hot temperature was almost evenly distributed, relative to the months. There was little to no frequency for extremely hot and cold temperatures. On the other hand, in the graph of 2013-2023, I noticed that hot temperatures were the most common, and the frequency of extremely hot went up by a lot, while the frequency of normal and cold temperatures went substantially down. 
2. What do you wonder?
	I wonder why this significant change occurred. Was it due to the significant increase of fossil fuels and global warming? Also, what is considered the “normal” temperature, and how is it determined? Did the idea of what is considered extremely hot and extremely cold change over time?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
	This impacts my community because just last december, there were days where the temperature was above 50. This is abnormal, especially in December, and I wonder if it will be considered normal in a few years due to the trend the graphs are showing. Also, global warming is a prevalent issue in our community, which is obvious from the graphs, and we really need to do something about it. 
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
	Temperature is on the rise!

raw_comment: Heightened Summer Heat: I notice that as time increases, and therefore comes closer to current day, the average temperature increases as well. From 1951-1980, the distribution of summer temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere was approximately normally distributed with the majority of days within the “normal” temperature range. However from 2013-2023, the graph has drastically shifted to the right with the majority of days in the “hot” and “extremely hot” temperature categories. This graph is right skewed. The first graph spans over 29 years while the second only shows data from a ten year period. I wonder, if the graphs were created on a ten year basis (for example, 1991-2001, 2002-2012, 2013-2023) would the graphs change as dramatically? I wonder what major inventions have led to this climate change? Could it include farming, cars, increased production? I wonder, is this data reflected similarly from other nations? Does this data match that of the southern hemisphere? I also am wondering, what specific temperatures constitute the categories “cold, normal, hot, and extremely hot”? As a New Hampshire resident, this directly impacts me and my community through our climate. The data shows summer temperatures of the Northern Hemisphere are increasingly warming up, impacting our lives in the summer. This climate change does not just impact what clothes we wear in the summer, it impacts available water, food availability, and even power use/consumption.

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
I notice that the temperature data shifts to the right and spread out quite significantly as time passes. The extreme temperatures go from being very minuscule, thin tails of the graph to the extremely hot temperatures nearing half of the data and frequency. The cold temperatures die out, changing from ⅓ of the frequency to an outlier amount of data. Another graphic that stood out to me was the color-coded map of temperature change over the Northern Hemisphere. The red extreme heat along the equator and mediterranean plus almost the entirety of the United States and Europe in abnormal yellow hot temperatures contrasts with the temperature map of 1951, showing yellow only in the desert regions of the United States and along the equator. 
I wonder how it would look to show the change in frequency of winter temperatures. 
Our area deals with heatwaves and other effects of climate change, like flooding and big storms, and our infrastructure and natural environment cannot handle the changing climate. The trend of the standard distribution of temperatures rising so significantly from 1951-2023 shows a disturbing rate of change and projected future.

raw_comment:
Miles Borne

1. What do you notice?
I notice 2 graphs that appear approximately normal distribution. On the bottom, there is a scale of temperatures that shows cold, Normal, and hot. It appears that in the graph of 1951-1980, there is an equal distribution of temperatures that are cold and hot. Then compared to the 2013-2023 graph the temperatures are not in the middle and don’t have an equal proportion of temperature that is hot and cold instead the middle of the graph is in the hot portion and there is only a tail of temperatures that are cold. 


2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how the temperature changes from year to year. Is it in a linear fashion changing the same every year? Or in an exponential fashion, starting slowly and then rapidly increasing?


3. What impact does this have on you and your community?


The impact that this has on my community is for one there used to be feet of snow in the winter, but now it’s just cold and there is no snow at all. The economy is also being hurt as things like skating snowboarding and even snowball fights are very rare and because of the temperature getting warmer, it’s hard. Also in the summer, this place is really lovely but because of how hot it’s getting there are simply some days where you shouldn’t go outside that often because of how hot it is. 


4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.


Too much summer?

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

1. I noticed that the data shifts toward the right throughout each graph as time goes on. The first graph is very evenly distributed whereas the second graph has more variation. I also noticed that between the years 1951 and 1980 temperatures in the hot range were on the far right tail of the distribution. And in the years 2013 and 2023 the temperatures in the hot range were right around the mean of the distribution. This shows that the average temperature has changed significantly as time has passed. 
2. One of my biggest questions is if there is a way to reverse this and if it is truly possible to reverse this. I also am curious to see the data from the years that preceded 1951, and if the numbers were even lower than what was shown on the far left of the distribution. 
3. Because I live in the Northern Hemisphere, where the data was collected from, it is clear that my community is affected by the change and increase in temperature. We also live on the seacoast where we can notice the weather changes clearly concerning the ocean. My family who lives in southern Asia has also seen effects that have been detrimental to their agriculture industry and their respective irrigation systems.

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

Hot and cold take up roughly equal amounts of the 1951-1980 graph but in the 2013-2023 graph, cold is a very small amount of the data. The graphs become more left-tailed as time goes on.

I wonder where the data was recorded. I wonder if this data is the average for the northern hemisphere.

Global warming affects the whole world. It’s been beginning to feel like summer earlier in the year and there’s been less snow in the winter.

	In the first graph , from 1951-1980, I noticed that the normal, cold, and hot temperature was almost evenly distributed, relative to the months. There was little to no frequency for extremely hot and cold temperatures. On the other hand, in the graph of 2013-2023, I noticed that hot temperatures were the most common, and the frequency of extremely hot went up by a lot, while the frequency of normal and cold temperatures went substantially down.

	I wonder why this significant change occurred. Was it due to the significant increase of fossil fuels and global warming? Also, what is considered the “normal” temperature, and how is it determined? Did the idea of what is considered extremely hot and extremely cold change over time?

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

1. What do you notice?
When looking at the graph, I notice a significant difference between temperatures from 1951-1980 and 2013-2023. In the earlier graph, it is split around half and half with hot and cold, and with no temperature being in the dark red. But for 2013-2023 I notice that there is almost no cold and that there is a lot of hot and extremely hot. Another thing to note is that on the 2013-2023 graph, the majority of the data is significantly higher than the “normal” temperature. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what is the cause of this significant increase in temperature. I wonder if global warming has any significant correlation with this increase in temperature. Is there any way to set the temperature back normal, or is this change permanent.

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
I notice that, as time goes on, the data is moving towards the right side of the graph, near the hot and extremely hot categories. The first graph has a thinner distribution and the distribution is wider in the second graph. The first graph is more evenly distributed than the second graph. The amount of hot summer temperatures seems equal to the amount of cold temperatures in the first graph, while there are many more hot and extremely hot days than cold days in the second graph. The first graph has a relatively normal distribution, while the second graph is skewed to the right.
I wonder what specifically is causing the data to read like this and why it continuously moves to the right. Is there any way to return the world to the state that it was in before? To have more even temperature distribution? What environmental impact does the changing temperatures have on Earth?
This has an impact on my community because I live in the northern hemisphere, where the data was collected. The graph is showing that the temperatures in the northern hemisphere are getting warmer as time goes on, which affects the area where I live. This explains why there has been so much rain and hotter temperatures in my area.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |
raw_comment:
I notice that the temperature data shifts to the right and spread out quite significantly as time passes. The extreme temperatures go from being very minuscule, thin tails of the graph to the extremely hot temperatures nearing half of the data and frequency. The cold temperatures die out, changing from ⅓ of the frequency to an outlier amount of data. Another graphic that stood out to me was the color-coded map of temperature change over the Northern Hemisphere. The red extreme heat along the equator and mediterranean plus almost the entirety of the United States and Europe in abnormal yellow hot temperatures contrasts with the temperature map of 1951, showing yellow only in the desert regions of the United States and along the equator. 
I wonder how it would look to show the change in frequency of winter temperatures. 
Our area deals with heatwaves and other effects of climate change, like flooding and big storms, and our infrastructure and natural environment cannot handle the changing climate. The trend of the standard distribution of temperatures rising so significantly from 1951-2023 shows a disturbing rate of change and projected future.
I would title the graph: “Rising Temperatures and Rising Climate Concerns.”

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |
raw_comment:
From the graph, I noticed that the most frequent temperature in 1951-1980 is normal summer temperatures, however, in 2013-2023 hot temperatures are most frequent. In 1951-1980 the graph is towards an average summer temperature as frequent with an equal relation to colder and hotter temperatures. The 2013-2023 data demonstrates how the temperatures have frequently become extremely hot. It is interesting to note how only a few decades have completely changed the frequent temperature of summer to trend hotter. This data suggests the presence of climate change and its impact on summer temperatures on the Northern Hemisphere. I wonder if the summer temperatures will continually trend towards frequent hot temperatures in the future. Will climate change policies such as the United States’ involvement in the Paris Agreement impact the data? This graph relates to my community and I because I live in the northern hemisphere. The rising temperatures impacts people's health and environmental implications. 

"Global Warming Heats up the Summer"

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |
raw_comment:
I notice that the average land temperatures across the Northern Hemisphere have changed drastically over the past 72 years. I notice that between 1951 and 1980 there were very rare extremely hot days however currently extremely hot days happen frequently. I notice that the amount of cold days has also drastically shrunk. I wonder how this graph will look in another 50 years. I wonder if there is any possibility of restoring temperatures to the state shown in the first graph, or if they only thing people can do is to work to prevent any further global warming(more than what is inevitable. I wonder how different the earth will be for my children and my children's children. I wonder how long global warming can go on at these rates before the earth is inhabitable. 
This relates to my community as I am currently witnessing the extreme state that global warming is in, and hope that I can be apart of the change in creating a greener earth. 
Say Goodbye to Cold Summer Days!(and potentially earth as we know it)

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that in the graph that summer temperatures have drastically changed in the sense that summers have gotten significantly hotter. In years 1951-1980 the temperature was roughly distributed normal throughout June-July- August in the Northern Hemisphere while in 2013-2023 the graph has shifted to the right meaning that temperature has gotten hotter. 
2. If the temperature in the future keeps rising, what can we expect for future generations? How much will temperatures rise if nothing is done? Why, in my opinion, isn't anything being done to at least lower temperatures? 
3. Even though it's only May, the temperatures are already rising, thus this is important to me and my community. Summer is coming. These heated, intense temperatures that are becoming higher every year are probably going to make this summer the hottest one yet. 
4. The World's on Fire

raw_comment: In these graphs, they are depicting how the average summer land temperatures across the Northern Hemisphere have changed over the past 72 years by comparing temperatures from 1951-1980 and temperatures from 2013-2023. In the first graph displaying the temperatures from 1951-1980, I noticed that normal temperatures were the most frequent, cold and hot temperatures were about the same frequency, and extremely hot temperatures were at a very low frequency. I wonder what temperatures are considered normal and how that is determined. However, when looking at the other graph measuring the temperature during years 2013-2023, I noticed a significant difference in the temperatures in comparison to the first graph. For example, the most frequent temperature was hot, the normal temperature’s frequency significantly decreased, and the extremely hot temperature’s frequency increased significantly whereas the cold temperature decreased. I wonder why this trend occurred and think that is caused by global warming. This relates to my community because I have noticed temperatures rising more and more and climate change is definitely a very prevalent issue. My headline for this graph would be: “Temperatures on the Rise”.

raw_comment:
These graphs show how the average summer land temperatures across the northern hemisphere have changed over the past 72 years (1951-2023). In the first graph (1951-1980), it is apparent that normal temperatures occur most often. However, cold and hot temperatures are both still very frequent and their frequencies are just about equal. Extremely cold and extremely hot temperatures are very rare during this time period. In the second graph (2013-2023) cold and even normal temperatures become significantly less frequent than they once were, and extremely cold temperatures are very rare. On the other hand, hot temperatures become more frequent, and extremely hot temperatures which were basically nonexistent in the first graph become much more common. I wonder why the graphs are such different shapes. The first graph is very high and narrow while the second graph is lower and wider. I can infer that this difference in temperatures is due to the range of the data because the second graph has a wider range of temperatures included in it. I wonder if climate change will continue to progress until the majority of temperatures are extremely hot. What will we do to stop this from happening? 
"You Are Going to Need More than a Fan this Summer"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.  Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Too Hot to Handle! Summer Temperatures Are on a Rise” by Josemanuel of Great Neck North High School, N.Y.; "Got AC? Summer's Coming and Only Getting Hotter" by Deven of Calif.; “Can We Beat The Heat? How Summers Are Getting Hotter And Hotter” by Kaatje of California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, "Changing Climates: How the World is Losing its Cool" by Aaron of San Luis Obispo and three from Perth Amboy High School, N.J. --  “Summers Skyrocket in Heat with Never Seen Before Temperatures” by Sarah, “The Northern Hemisphere Kettle Has Heated Up” by Santiago and “Summer Surge: Temperatures At An All-Time High” by Emily.
 
Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that includes this graph.  Also in the Reveal are a summary of the topic, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.
 
This is the last featured graph of the school year.  Please return in early September when we will have more graphs in which you can see yourself.
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who hopes we continue to try hard to reverse the temperature trend, and Melanie Battles of Brooklyn, who thinks it’s an unsurprising coincidence that in NYC today, it’s 22ºF above the daily average high temperature!

raw_comment:
I notice that average summer temperatures in Northern Hemisphere have increased significantly since the 1950s. Over a mere ten year period (2013-2023), the average summer temperature rose to be in the "hot" rather than "normal" range. Interestingly, the graphs have also changed in terms of distribution. The data points are more extreme, leading to a wider curve. Also, the Northern Hemisphere now experiences "extremely hot" weather, when from 1951-1980 this was virtually nonexistent. 

I wonder if climate change has precipitated these changes. Anthropogenic activity is known to cause more extreme weather patterns, so I am curious if the wide distribution of temperature from 2013-2023 has the same cause. I also wonder if "normal" temperatures are in the context of the Earth's history, or simply 1951-1980. Is it normal for the preindustrial era, too?

This relates to me and my community because rising summer temperatures makes the Northern Hemisphere less hospitable, especially for those with existing medical conditions. If extremely hot temperatures persist, people might be encouraged to migrate toward the cooler poles. Rising temperatures could also hurt species diversity, as natives might not be able to survive in different conditions.

"A Midsummer Night's HEAT"

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
This graph depicts the temperature of the northern hemisphere from July to August from 1950 until 2023. The graph compares how the temperature rates have gradually changed over time. In the 1951 to 1980 time period, there was a much higher rate of moderate temperatures. Cold and hot temperature rates of frequency were pretty even. However, from 2013 to 2023, the hot temperature spanning into extremely hot temperatures has become more common. In present days, cold and neutral temperatures are becoming rare in the northern hemisphere. With the effects of global warming at hand, many activist groups fight for ways to end the harm humans are doing to Earth which has made temperatures scarily increase. Yet, if their efforts are implemented will they work? Will temperatures start to drop again? Or are global warming and the extremely hot temperatures unwavering from irreversible damage? This relates to my community because we all are negatively affected by increasing temperatures. The reservoir by my home that has been used by the public for decades has been closed the past few summers because of dangerous algae blooms caused by extremely hot temperatures. Many people in the area, without even swimming, have gotten sick from these blooms. 
“Up Next: Only Hot Days Ahead”

1) I notice that summer temperatures from 2013-2023 are less cold and more hot, even treading to extremely hot compared to temperatures in 1951-1980, where they were fairly split between cold and hot. Looking at the graphs we can see this clearly as the graph from 1951-1980 is more centered and has no tails while the graph from 2013-2023 has a left tail and therefore is skewed to the left, which in this case it means more hot temperatures during the summer.

If it already feels like this in spring, then imagine when summer actually comes.

4) Summer Surge: Temperatures At An All-Time High

raw_comment:
I noticed that in the first graph showing the temperatures for 1951-1980 had a peak in the normal temperature range and had a minuscule amount of extremely hot days. In the second graph showing the temperatures for 2013-2023, the graph had a peak in the hot temperature range and around ⅔ of the temperatures for that time period were within the extremely hot range. I noticed that as more years passed, the hotter the days got during the summertime. I wonder where in the Northern Hemisphere these temperatures were recorded, because there is a difference in temperatures during the summer months in New England compared to somewhere like Florida or Texas. I would also wonder what role climate change has had on these temperatures and if there are any correlations between the increasing temperatures during certain summers and the rate of climate change. I also wonder what the graphs define as a “normal”, “extremely hot”, “hot”,  or “cold” temperature. There is no numerical value provided for each category, just a description which can be interpreted differently by each person. With rising temperatures each summer this can have an impact on the environment and the people. With the rising temperatures this can change rainfall patterns which impacts the plants and animals around us during the summer. Severe increases in temperatures will increase the evaporation rates which will create longer and more severe droughts for communities. 
“Climate Change: Weather You Like it or Not”

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

What do you notice?

I notice that the temperate during summer is getting hotter and became drastically hotter between 1980 and 2013. The temperate is reaching numbers in 2023 that it has never reached before. There is also becoming increasingly fewer normal and cold days.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why the temperate has been increasing so rapidly and if this has anything to do with global warming. I wonder how the graph would look differently if it showed data from the southern hemisphere instead.

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because the increasing temperature could have very negative effects on my community, and we must do all that we can to help. It starts with me, you, and all individuals. If not us, then who? If not now, then when?

Too Hot Too Handle: Temperatures Are Rising Off The Charts!

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
I notice how drastically the temperature of the summer season has changed over the past 72 years in the Northern Hemisphere. From 1951 to 1980 the majority of the temperature readings were “normal”, but it seems as though the longer time passed, that “hot” and “extremely hot” temperatures became the new normal, and the “normal” temperatures fell into the minority if the data.
I wonder what the actual temperatures are, like what is the range for “cold”, “normal”, “hot”, and “extremely hot”. I also wonder why people still refuse to acknowledge that climate change is happening when data like this prevails. 
I live in a progressive community so this kind of information is important to everyone. I think these kinds of statistics make people want to change, become more aware of the issue, and do their part to combat climate change.
Alternative Title: “It’s like a Million Degrees... Literally”

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
1. While looking at the graphs I notice that  over the past 72 years the average summer land temperatures have gone from cold to hot then extremely hot. From 1950 to 1980, the temperature of the lands varied from cold, hot, and extremely hot. However in 2020 the graph shows that there is about a 80% increase in the hottere days. The 1951-1980 graph has a normal distribution with the temperatures being around the mean of 1 degree celsius above the baseline. Comparing the tails of the graph shows a trend that is going on. The upper extreme of  2 degrees celsius from 1951-1980 is now in the bulk of the 2013-2023 distribution. 
2. This is concerning seeing how much hotter it is getting by the years. I wonder how they determined what is extremely hot and what is normal. I wonder what can we do if anything to slow down these increasing temperatures and what is influencing them to increase at such a rapid rate. 
3. This has an impact on our community because as the years go by and the temperature gets hotter, it can affect future generations. Such an increase in temperature can put a lot of nature at risk and habitats for wildlife. 
4. You're Gonna Need an AC

raw_comment: I noticed the temperatures during 1951-1980 in the Northern Hemisphere had a somewhat even split between cold, normal, and hot. This pattern took a drastic change from 2013-2023 when the whole graph shifted to the right. This shift increased the hot and extremely hot days but lessened the cold and normal days. I wonder how this graph will look in the next ten years, and if anything is being done to battle this. The increase in extremely hot temperatures affects my community tremendously. It is not good for our Earth to be facing such hot temperatures and no regulation with cold/normal temperatures. With the temperatures so high, it increases the chance of drought, plants dying, and heat exhaustion for humans. All these factors decrease our ability to thrive in our community. The title I came up with: “Sizzling Stats: the harsh truth about our days!"

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

The proportion of days that have been extremely hot has risen greatly in the decade from 2013-2023 compared to 1951-1980. 

What are the temperatures categorized as hot or extremely hot? What time of day was the temperature recorded at? 

This is incredibly important to my community, and also to the world. There is no denying that humans have made an incredible impact on the rise in global temperatures and climate change overall. This impact can mean that temperatures around the world, and in my town will continue to rise and cause harm to the environment and many other factors than can be affected.

raw_comment:
These two graphs display the Northern Hemisphere's summer land temperatures from 1950 to 2023. The summer temperatures depict the June-July-August range. I noticed that in 1951-1980 the temperatures were cold and in 2013-2023 the temperatures ranged from hot to extremely hot. Is global warming the catalyst for the temperature rise? Does the rise in temperatures only apply to the Northern Hemisphere and if the data showed other Hemispheres would the results be different? I wonder what else could be the cause of the temperature rise. I think the graph should show the causes of the temperature rise to help the data be clearer. This relates to me and my community because I have noticed in my community the rise in temperatures during the summer compared to other years. Also, around the world, the summer heat has devastatingly affected communities by the increased wildfires. 

Title: Its Getting Hot In Here

- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.

This relates to my community because I have seen frequent  temperature changes where I live during the summer and I have seen it get much hotter within the last few years.

This is the last graph of the school year.  Please return in early September when we will have more graphs in which you can see yourself.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |
raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is how many "Extremely hot" days there are in the 2013-2023 graph. The extremely hot category is barely noticeable in the 1951-1980 base period. It would mean that the hottest days of today didn't even exist back then. The extremely cold category also reaches out a little further in the 2013-2023 graph, meaning there's some evidence that even the coldest days of today were a little worse than before. 
I wonder if 30 years before the 1951-1980 base period were any cooler. It might help provide some context to the graph we see. I imagine prior to 1951 wasn't that much cooler, but it would still be nice to see it compared to 1951-1980. Another thing I wonder is why the data collected was only in the Northern Hemisphere. Was it too difficult to also collect similar data in the Southern Hemisphere during the base period?
This relates to me personally since as the days get hotter in our modern world we all generally suffer more for it. The extremely hot days mean were more at risk for dangerous wildfires (and other fires) since the majority of terrain is so dry for a long period of the year due to the extreme heat. We have to think of ways to adapt in order to cope with the fact our world is hotter. A good name for the graph would be: "Days Are Hotter Today Compared to 30 to 50 Years Ago", or "The Cost of Living In the Modern World: Extreme Heat."

raw_comment:
Interesting title: Visualizing the Alarming Rise in Northern Hemisphere Summer Temperatures

The two area graphs provide a striking visual comparison of summer temperature distributions in the Northern Hemisphere across different 30-year periods, revealing an alarming warming trend. The 1951-1980 graph approximates a normal distribution, with temperatures symmetrically clustered around the mean of 1°C above baseline. Fast forward to 2013-2023, and the curve has shifted significantly to the right and flattened out, with the peak now around 1.5°C above baseline. From living in San Luis Obispo, California, I've witnessed the changing climate firsthand, with summers growing hotter and more prolonged.
Comparing the tails reveals an alarming trend: the former upper extreme of 2°C from 1951-1980 is now squarely in the bulk of the 2013-2023 distribution. In San Luis Obispo, we've experienced the consequences, from severe droughts to extended wildfire seasons. Graphs like these make the reality of climate change starkly visible, underscoring the urgency of addressing this warming trend. They remind us of the need for our community to take action and build a more sustainable future.

raw_comment:
I notice from the graphs that the frequency of "normal" temperatures has severely decreased in the last 72 years. I've noticed that what was considered a hot average temperature from 1951-1980 has now become what is the norm in the Northern Hemisphere. I also noticed that there is much more variability in the graph now. In the base period the temperatures were heavily centered at the normal temperature with small tails on both sides. While in the modern plot the ranges of temperatures is much greater with a very large right tail insinuating that there are much higher temperatures now than there was then. 

I wonder why the shape of the plot has changed and not just the temperatures itself. Knowing about global warming and the production of fossil fuels, the temperature increase does not surprise me but the idea that the distributions are different shapes is puzzling. I wonder if that can be attributed to exponential growth. I also wonder how the Northern Hemisphere compares to the southern hemisphere and if there are similar trends there or if possibly they are opposite trends. 

This relates to my community because from a few environmental classes I've taken, I learned that this massive temperature increase is putting a lot of nature at risk and making habitats and species die. As someone who loves to travel and see nature it is important to me that the animals and plants around us are being taken care of by us.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed was the peak of the graph shifting from left to right, indicating that the temperature increased over time. The next thing I noticed was how the graph started to shift from a visibily normal graph to one that was skewed right. I think that is also important to note that as the graph's peak moves from normal to hot, it also lowers, indicating more that temperatures are varying more. So while colder temperatures are becoming less common, the range of the temperatures is increasing, which tells you just how fast extreme temperatures are on the rise. Something that I wonder is if this animated graph would be similar for the years 1900-1950. I wonder if temperatures were always on the rise like this. 
This information affects the entire world, and thus also my community. This acts as just another reminder for us a community, and as a population to do our best in preventing global increasing temperatures. A name for this graph could be "Wow! It's getting hot in here! Well, everywhere actually"

raw_comment:
1. When first looking at the two graphs, the drastic increase in temperature changes that have occurred in less than 75 years jumped out at me. The graph displaying the Northern Hemisphere temperatures from 1951-1980 appears to follow a normal distribution, where cold and hot temperatures seem to be evenly distributed on both sides. However, the graph below showing the temperatures from 2013-2023 has a right skewed distribution with hot and extremely hot temperatures taking up most of the graph. This indicates just how quickly temperature is evolving to be hotter and hotter and will continue to do so over time.

2. Something I wonder is what we can do to slow down these rapidly increasing temperatures. For example, if everyone switched to only driving electric cars or even having hybrid cars, how quickly would we see the results of its impact on the environment? 

3. These increasing temperatures severely impact our community as the earth will continue to heat up and affect our future generations. I'm concerned about how high the temperature will be for my future kids and grandkids and how that will impact their lifestyle. 

4. "Hotter Horizons: Earth's Escalating Climate (1951-2023)"

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
Watching the animation the first thing that became clear was that when comparing 1951-1980 to 2013-2023 the number of hot and extremely hot days has dramatically increased, while at the same time, there is a substantial reduction of cold days. This is because over time the curve not only became shorter and wider but experienced a left shift. This indicates that the median temperature went from being “Normal” in the ’50s to being “Hot” in modern times. 
I'm curious exactly how this data was recorded. The subtitle says it is the temperature in the Northern Hemisphere, so is it fair to assume it is an average of every country’s or every state/province’s temperature? Additionally, I am curious as to the exact range of temperatures that constitute each temperature label. To me hot is any temperature over 80 degrees, but I wonder if they used a more conservative scale with hot starting at 90 degrees. This applies to me since I live in an area particularly susceptible to fires. Higher temperatures mean dryer brush and higher fire risk, which directly impacts my community's and my safety. I would title this graph “Rising Temperatures Means Sweltering Summers.”

- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

raw_comment:
There seems to be an increase in land temperature. From 1950 to 1980, the temperature of the lands varied equally from cold to normal to hot. 2020 shows that over 80% of the entire amount is made up of hotter and more humid areas. This raises serious concerns and is very perplexing.
I'm curious how they determined what constitutes a severe heat and what is deemed normal. How they are obtaining these temps is another question I have. Are they measuring the average temperature throughout the Northern Hemisphere or are they measuring the temperature in a specific location?
Even though it's still early May, the temperatures are already beginning to rise into the 70s and even 80s, thus this speaks to me and my neighborhood. There are days when the heat is so intense that it feels like summer has arrived.
Weather Forecasts: The Evolution of Summer Temperatures
